title: A cheerful face
hook: Shammai: receive everyone with a cheerful face (Pirkei Avot 1:15)
tomorrow: Hillel says don't judge someone until you've done what, exactly?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hillel's three questions, and a long debate in the Talmud that ends on examining your deeds, now. If not now, when?

People who train front-desk staff sometimes say a caller can hear a smile down the phone. The rabbis said something close, and from an unexpected mouth. Shammai, the sage with a name for strictness, Hillel's rival, has a saying in Pirkei Avot. Make your study a fixed habit. Say little and do much. And receive every person with a cheerful face. In Hebrew, sever panim yafot. That's the rule about your face. And it comes from the man at the center of a sharp scene in the Talmud.
screen: `YOU CAN HEAR A SMILE.` → `SHAMMAI, THE STRICT ONE.` → `SAY LITTLE, DO MUCH.` → `RECEIVE EVERYONE WITH A CHEERFUL FACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the scene, from the Talmud. A man who wants to become a Jew comes to Shammai and says: convert me, on one condition. Teach me the whole Torah while I stand on one foot. Shammai pushes him away with the builder's measuring stick in his hand. The man goes to Hillel, who says: what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor. That's the whole Torah; the rest is commentary. Go and learn it. So the man remembered for pushing someone away is the one who taught the cheerful face. Some teachers read that as a man who knew his own edge and wrote himself the rule he needed. Either way, the rule stands in Pirkei Avot under his name. How you receive a person is part of what you give them. Avot de-Rabbi Natan spells it out: give someone every good gift in the world with a sour face, and Scripture counts it as if you gave nothing. Receive them with a cheerful face, even with nothing in your hands, and it's as if you gave every good gift. The face isn't decoration. It's the first thing you hand to anyone who walks in.
screen: `TEACH ME ON ONE FOOT.` · `SHAMMAI PUSHES HIM AWAY.` · `THE WELCOME IS PART OF THE GIFT.` · then, large: `A CHEERFUL FACE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and notice your face from the inside. Let the forehead go smooth, unclench the jaw, let the tongue rest, and soften the skin around the eyes, the place a real welcome starts. Then hold someone in mind, someone you'll see today, and let your face greet them, gently, as the bell rings.
A cheerful face: sever panim yafot, Shammai's rule for how to receive every person who comes to you.
Here's the line: a cheerful face, the gift you can give with empty hands. Day three of the sayings, done.

fork.setup: a neighbor drops by while you're in a foul mood. you can give her the jar of jam she wanted, or just a warm hello. what does Avot de-Rabbi Natan say counts?
options: the warm face; a gift handed over sourly counts as if nothing was given.
the jam; actions count, and the face is only a feeling.
neither; Shammai's rule only covers guests who come to study.
fork.reveal: the welcome is part of the gift. with a cheerful face, even empty hands give something.

original.note: Hebrew, Pirkei Avot 1:15: a pleasant, cheerful face, the way to receive every person.

trapdoor: what you thought: smile more, a customer-service tip.
what it means: in Jewish teaching, how you receive a person is part of what you give them, so the face itself is a kindness.
what a scholar hears: Avot de-Rabbi Natan 13 on Shammai's saying: every good gift with a downcast face counts as nothing, a cheerful face with nothing counts as every good gift.
guess: a warm, open welcome for every person who comes
a big grin worn no matter how you feel inside
a calm face that hides every feeling from others

chat.says: got thursday morning off for ray. but a coworker says i've had a doom face at the desk all week. does it matter?
options: It matters. Shammai: receive everyone with a cheerful face. The welcome is part of the gift.
Not really. Only what you do for patients counts; your face is just a feeling.
Not this week. The rule is for when life's going well, not when you're worried.
chat.meaning: Shammai's rule puts the welcome inside the gift, and Avot de-Rabbi Natan says a gift with a sour face counts as nothing.
